# bytes

Raw octets — binary data that can also be treated as ASCII-range text.

## Overview

`bytes` is the low-level member of the text family: a mutable sequence of **octets** with no symbol
interpretation. The element is the [`byte`](byte.md).

| type | representation | mutability | indexing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bytes` | raw octets, no symbol interpretation | **mutable** | O(1) by octet |
| `string` | Unicode text in compact UTF-8 | immutable | O(n) by symbol — see [string](string.md) |
| `runes` | Unicode text as a symbol array | mutable | O(1) by symbol — see [runes](runes.md) |

The line between `bytes` and the symbol types is **encoding**. Members that need symbol classes — `upper`,
`lower`, `case_fold`, the casing family — do not exist on `bytes`: interpreting an octet as a cased letter
means assuming an encoding.

```go
bytes("héllo").len()                // => 6 — octets — é is two
bytes("héllo").upper()              // Error: invalid_method: type bytes has no method upper
bytes("héllo").string().upper()     // => "HÉLLO" — decode, then the symbol work
```

The edge members `first([d])`, `last([d])`, `min([d])` and `max([d])` take the optional trailing default; an
empty receiver has no answer to give, so without one they raise `invalid_value`. No `sum`/`avg` — see the
exclusions.

```go
bytes("bca").first()        // => byte(98)
bytes("bca").min()          // => byte(97)
bytes("").first(b'?')       // => byte(63)
bytes("").first()           // Error: invalid_value: (first) empty sequence
```

Decoding is total too: `bytes` → `string`/`runes` never raises — an octet that is not part of valid UTF-8 rides
through as its escape rune (U+DC80–U+DCFF) and converts back to the same octet.

There is no `.int()`/`.float()`/`.decimal()`/`.bool()`/`.time()` on `bytes` — octets are not text until
decoded. Parse through the decode: `bytes("42").string().int()` → `42`. There are no `.dict()`/`.record()`
conversions either (octets are never key/value entries), and no `.byte()` (`bytes([65])` is a sequence;
its element is `b[0]`).

## Literals and construction

The literal form is `b"..."`, with the same escapes as `string` literals plus raw octet escapes:

```go
b"ab"               // => bytes([97, 98])
b"\x00\xff"         // => bytes([0, 255])
```

**`bytes` is a mutable sequence — but a literal is an immutable constant.**:
the *type* is writable, and `b"..."` is a compile-time constant of that type. Its content
is fixed in the source, so the compiler stores it once in the bytecode's static pool and every evaluation
loads that one shared value; `bytes` is most often constant text or a fixed byte pattern — a magic prefix,
a separator, a key — which is what the short `b"..."` form is for. When you want a buffer, you construct one:

```go
type_name(b"ab")            // => "immutable-bytes"
l := b"abc"
l[0] = b'X'                 // Error: not_assignable: type immutable-bytes does not support assignment ...

m := bytes(b"abc")          // a constructor always builds a new, writable body
m[0] = b'X'
m                           // => bytes([88, 98, 99]) — the literal is untouched
m = b"abc".copy()           // the same thing, spelled as a copy
m = bytes("abc")            // or build it from a string
```

`bytes(...)` is both the conversion (one argument) and the count constructor (two arguments): `bytes(x, n)` is
`bytes(x)` repeated `n` times, so `bytes(b'\x00', n)` is the preallocation spelling:

```go
bytes("héllo")          // => bytes([104, 195, 169, 108, 108, 111]) — UTF-8 octets of the text
bytes([104, 105])       // => bytes([104, 105]) — an array of in-range ints or bytes, element-wise
bytes([b'h', b'i'])     // => bytes([104, 105])
bytes([300])            // Error: conversion — not an octet
bytes(b'\x07')          // => bytes([7]) — a byte is one octet — any octet
bytes('8')              // => bytes([56]) — a rune contributes its UTF-8 octets — not the digit 8
bytes(5)                // Error: conversion: cannot convert int to bytes: no conversion exists
bytes("ab", 2)          // => bytes([97, 98, 97, 98]) — the count form: bytes(x).repeat(n)
bytes(b'\x00', 3)       // => bytes([0, 0, 0]) — the preallocation: n explicit fill octets
```

Encoding is total — every text-ish value has UTF-8 octets — so `string`/`runes` → `bytes` never fails.
Non-text scalars have no direct octet reading: `(3).bytes()` does not exist — go through the text,
`(3).string().bytes()`.

## Indexing and slicing

All positions are octet positions. Negative indices count from the end; slices clamp. Slicing can split a
multi-octet symbol — `bytes` does not know or care:

```go
bytes("héllo")[1]           // => byte(195) — the first octet of é
bytes("abc")[-1]            // => byte(99)
bytes("héllo").slice(0, 3)  // => bytes([104, 195, 169])
```

Element writes (`m[i] = b'x'`) mutate the shared body and are visible through every alias; on a frozen or
literal value they raise.

## Operators

| operator | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `+` | concatenation; the **receiver** (left operand) decides the result type |
| `-` | removes **every** occurrence of the right operand (leftmost, non-overlapping); acceptance equals `+`'s |
| `*` | exactly `repeat(n)`: the right operand is a **count**, not content. No reflected direction — `n * b` raises |
| `==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=` | content-based, octet by octet — compares across `string`/`runes`/`bytes` by text content |
| `in` | membership: `x in b` uses `contains`' value readings (element or run); raises on an unacceptable operand — never a silent `false` |

Operand acceptance — every accepted operand is text content, encoded into octets. Encoding is total, so
`bytes` accepts every text-ish operand unconditionally:

| right operand | reading |
| --- | --- |
| `bytes` | its octets, verbatim |
| `string` / `runes` | its UTF-8 octets |
| `rune` | its 1–4 UTF-8 octets |
| `byte` | that octet |
| `int` | **raises** — arithmetic keeps the numeric reading of `+`/`-`; the member forms (`push`, `append`) take an in-range int |
| `bool` / `float` / `decimal` | raises — ambiguous as text |
| `int` (`*` only) | a repeat **count** — `b * n` is exactly `b.repeat(n)`; there is no reflected `n * b` |
| `array` / `range` / `dict` / callables | raises — the text types accept only text content. `bytes("ab") + [1, 2]` → `[bytes([97, 98]), 1, 2]` is not an exception to that: `bytes` declines and the array answers `+` by prepending it (see [array](array.md)) |

```go
bytes("ab") + "cd"          // => bytes([97, 98, 99, 100]) — bytes receiver → bytes
bytes("ab") + u"cd"         // => bytes([97, 98, 99, 100])
bytes("ab") + 'é'           // => bytes([97, 98, 195, 169]) — a rune contributes its UTF-8 octets
bytes("ab") + b'\xff'       // => bytes([97, 98, 255]) — any octet — no ASCII limit on this side
bytes("ab") + 98            // Error: invalid_binary_operator: bytes + int
bytes("ab") + [1]           // => [bytes([97, 98]), 1] — bytes declines; the array prepends it
bytes("ab") - [1]           // Error: invalid_binary_operator: bytes - array
"ab" + bytes("cd")          // => "abcd" — string receiver → decodes the bytes
"ab" + bytes([255])         // => "ab\xff" — the octet is carried through as its escape
b'a' + bytes("bc")          // => bytes([97, 98, 99]) — a scalar on the left takes the sequence's type

bytes("abcabc") - "bc"      // => bytes([97, 97]) — every occurrence
bytes("banana") - b'a'      // => bytes([98, 110, 110])
bytes("héllo") - 'é'        // => bytes([104, 108, 108, 111]) — removes the 2-octet run
bytes("abc") - 98           // Error: invalid_binary_operator: bytes - int

bytes("ab") * 3             // => bytes([97, 98, 97, 98, 97, 98]) — the count form of repeat
b"ab" * 2                   // => bytes([97, 98, 97, 98]) — a literal answers a new, mutable value
3 * bytes("ab")             // Error: invalid_binary_operator: int * bytes   (no reflected direction)
bytes("ab") * b'\x03'       // Error: invalid_binary_operator: bytes * byte   (the operand is a count, not content)

bytes("ab") == "ab"         // => true
bytes("ab") == u"ab"        // => true
bytes("ab") < bytes("b")    // => true

b'a' in bytes("ab")         // => true — element
"bc" in bytes("abc")        // => true — run of octets
'é' in bytes("héllo")       // => true — the rune's 2-octet run
97 in bytes("abc")          // => true — an in-range int reads as one octet
300 in bytes("abc")         // Error: invalid_value — not an octet — never a silent false
```

A callable on the right of `in` raises: an operator operand is always a value — the predicate reading is
spelled `contains(f)` / `any(f)`.

## Argument dispatch — the argument's type selects the reading

Every member that matches or adds content reads its arguments from one menu:

| argument | reading |
| --- | --- |
| absent | the **blank set** (below) |
| function | predicate — it gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)) |
| `string` / `runes` / `bytes` | a **run** — a contiguous octet subsequence (text contributes its UTF-8 octets) |
| `rune` / `byte` / `int` | one **element** where it fits: a byte always; an int in `0`–`255` (members only — operators refuse int); a rune only if its encoding is one octet (ASCII) |
| several arguments (match side) | a **set** — "∈ the set"; homogeneous: all elements or all runs, mixing raises |
| several arguments (add side: `append`/`prepend`) | operands in order — mixing freely is the point |

A multi-octet rune is still fine wherever a **run** is accepted (`append`, `contains`, `replace`, ...) — it
reads as its 1–4 octets; only the strictly one-element slots (`push`, `insert` items, pad fills, `map`
results) refuse it.

Run matching is leftmost and non-overlapping; in a variadic run set, the longest wins at a tie.

## Decoding is total

`bytes` is the type with nothing to validate — every octet is a valid octet, which is why it carries
`is_ascii()` but no `is_valid()`. Decoding *out* of it never fails either: an octet that is not a symbol
becomes its reserved escape in the text, and converting back returns the same octet.

```go
b = bytes([0x61, 0xFF, 0x62])
b.string().bytes() == b         // => true
b.runes().bytes() == b          // => true
b.is_ascii()                    // => false
b.string().is_valid()           // => false — ask the type that can answer it
```

See [string: Undecodable octets](string.md#undecodable-octets) for the model, and note the one boundary that
is **not** total: `json.encode` on text holding escapes raises, while `json.encode(b)` on the bytes
themselves is always fine (base64).

## The blank set

The text types share one notion of insignificant content — **NUL ∪ whitespace** — projected into each
type's element domain. For `bytes` that is NUL plus **ASCII whitespace**: the fixed octet set
`{0x00, ' ', '\t', '\n', '\r', '\v', '\f'}` — all the whitespace a single octet can express. Deciding
anything wider would require decoding, which octets never get: an NBSP's octets (`0xC2 0xA0`) are
**content** here, not blank. The default pad fill is the canonical member of the set, the space octet.

The no-argument form of a member reads through this set:

- `trim()` / `trim_start()` / `trim_end()` strip blank octets; `split()` separates on runs of them.
- The queries — `contains()`, `any()`, `count()`, `index()`, `index_last()`, `all()` — ask about
**significant** (non-blank) octets.
- `keep()` keeps the significant octets; `remove()` removes the blank ones — two actions, same answer.

```go
bytes("  hi \t ").trim()            // => bytes([104, 105])
bytes([0, 104, 0]).trim()           // => bytes([104]) — NUL is blank
bytes("\u00a0x\u00a0").trim()       // => bytes([194, 160, 120, 194, 160]) — NBSP octets are content
bytes("  a b \t c ").split()        // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]
bytes("  ").contains()              // => false — no significant octet
bytes(" a b ").count()              // => 2
bytes("  ab").index()               // => 2 — first significant octet
bytes(" a b ").remove()             // => bytes([97, 98])
bytes("42").pad_start(5)            // => bytes([32, 32, 32, 52, 50]) — default fill = the space octet
```

## In-place twins

`bytes` is a mutable-body type, so every eligible transform has an `_in_place` twin that mutates the shared
body (visible through every alias), **returns the receiver**, and raises kind `not_mutable` on a frozen
receiver:

```go
t := bytes("  hi  ")
alias := t
t.trim_in_place()               // => bytes([104, 105]) — returns the receiver
// alias is now bytes([104, 105]) too

fz := bytes("abc").freeze()
fz.push_in_place(b'x')          // Error: not_mutable: (push_in_place) type immutable-bytes is immutable
fz.append(b'd')                 // => bytes([97, 98, 99, 100]) — the copying form works on a frozen receiver
```

The unsuffixed name is always the safe, copying form. `slice` has no twin (`slice_view` names the saving);
`repeat` has none (its result is n × the receiver); `map`/`split`/`partition`/`chunk` have none.

## Exclusions

- **`upper` / `lower` / `case_fold` / `title_case` and the identifier casings** — symbol classes and case
mappings assume an encoding, which octets never get; decode first: `.string().upper()`.
- **`sum` / `avg`** — elements are octets, not numbers; the checksum spelling is
`b.reduce(0, func(acc, x) { return acc + x.int() })`.
- **`join`** — the collection-as-receiver render lives on `array`/`range`; spell it
`b.array().join(",")` if you want an octet listing.
- **Scalar conversions (`.int()`, `.float()`, `.decimal()`, `.bool()`, `.time()`)** — octets are not text
until decoded; `string` is the gateway: `.string().int()`.
- **`.dict()` / `.record()`** — octets are never key/value entries.
- **`.byte()`** — wrapping/unwrapping is not conversion; the element access is `b[0]`.
- **`fields`** — no-arg `split()` *is* the whitespace splitter.
- **`copy_shallow` / `freeze_shallow`** — elements are scalars; there is no second level to stop at.

## Callbacks

A member that takes a function — the predicate reading of the match members, `map`, `flat_map`, `for_each`, `reduce`
— calls it in the **fewest form it accepts**, read from the callable's arity and whether it is variadic, never from
what kind of callable it is:

- a per-element callback gets the element when it accepts one argument, else `(index, element)`; anything else
raises;
- a `reduce` callback gets `(acc, element)` when it accepts two arguments, else `(acc, index, element)`; anything
else raises.

So `func(x, ...rest)` and `func(...args)` get the element, and a builtin or a bound member is a callback like any
other (`min` and `"abc".contains` accept one argument). A lambda is the one way to call a callable in another form —
choose the form, reorder, fix or drop arguments:

```go
bytes("abc").count(func(i, c) { return i > 0 })            // => 2 — accepts two, not one
bytes("abc").index(func(c, ...rest) { return c == 'b' })  // => 1 — accepts one: the element
bytes("abcd").keep("bd".contains)                         // => bytes([98, 100])
```

<a id="all"></a>
### `all(...x) -> bool`

Report whether every element matches a value, a set or a predicate; with no argument, whether every element is significant; see [`any`](#any).

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

<a id="any"></a>
### `any(...x) -> bool`

Report whether some element matches a value, a set or a predicate; with no argument, whether any element is significant.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`any`/`all` take a value, a function, or nothing; a run argument raises.

```go
bytes("abc").any(func(x) { return x == b'c' })       // => true
bytes("abc").all(func(x) { return x >= b'a' })       // => true
```

<a id="append"></a>
### `append(...xs) -> bytes`

Add the arguments at the back as whole operands, each text operand contributing its UTF-8 octets.

`append`/`prepend` take whole operands in order — `x.append(a, b)` ≡ `x + a + b` — mixing runs and elements
freely; each text operand contributes its UTF-8 octets.

```go
bytes("ab").append("cd", 'é', b'\xff', u"z")  // => bytes([97, 98, 99, 100, 195, 169, 255, 122])
bytes("cd").prepend("ab", b'x')     // => bytes([97, 98, 120, 99, 100])
```

<a id="append_in_place"></a>
### `append_in_place(...xs) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `append`.

<a id="array"></a>
### `array([default]) -> array`

Answer the octets as an array of `byte` elements, without decoding.

`.array()` materialises the octets as `byte` elements — no decoding.

```go
bytes("hi").array()         // => [byte(104), byte(105)]
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="bytes"></a>
### `bytes([default]) -> bytes`

Answer a new, independent, mutable copy, exactly `bytes(b)` / `b.copy()`.

```go
bytes("ab").bytes()         // a NEW, independent, mutable copy — same as bytes(b), not the receiver
b"ab".bytes()               // the writable-buffer idiom: a literal's constant body, copied
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="chunk"></a>
### `chunk(n) -> array`

Split into `bytes` of up to `n` octets, each a copy.

`chunk` copies, [`chunk_view`](#chunk_view) shares.

```go
bytes("abcde").chunk(2)         // => [bytes([97, 98]), bytes([99, 100]), bytes([101])]
```

<a id="chunk_view"></a>
### `chunk_view(n) -> array`

Split into `bytes` of up to `n` octets sharing the receiver's storage, each marked as a view; see [`chunk`](#chunk).

<a id="contains"></a>
### `contains(...x) -> bool`

Report whether an element, a run, a member of a set or a predicate match occurs; with no argument, whether any element is significant.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`contains` takes the full menu: element, run, homogeneous variadic set, predicate, or absent.
`contains(fn)` ≡ `any(fn)` and `contains()` ≡ `any()`.

```go
bytes("héllo").contains("éll")      // => true — its UTF-8 octet run
bytes("abc").contains(b'x', b'b')   // => true — set
bytes("abc").contains(func(x) { return x > b'b' })   // => true
```

### `copy() -> bytes`

Answer an independent, mutable copy.

([callbacks](#callbacks)).

```go
bytes("banana").count(b'a')         // => 3
```

<a id="flat_map"></a>
### `flat_map(fn) -> bytes`

Map each element through the callback, then concatenate: a run result splices in, `undefined` is dropped.

The callback gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)).

```go
bytes("ab").flat_map(func(x) { return x == b'a' ? "aa" : undefined })   // => bytes([97, 97])
```

### `for_each(fn) -> bytes`

Call the callback on every element — always a **full pass**, its return value ignored — and return the receiver.

The callback gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)).

<a id="has_suffix"></a>
### `has_suffix(x, ...more) -> bool`

Report whether the `bytes` value ends with the element or run, or with any of a set of them; see [`has_prefix`](#has_prefix).

<a id="index"></a>
### `index([x[, default]]) -> int`

Answer the first position of a match of an element, a run or a predicate, or `undefined` (the `default` when given) on a miss.

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

The only two locators; answers are **octet positions**, directly usable with `[i]`, `[i:j]`, `slice()`. A miss
answers `undefined` — never `-1` — or the optional trailing default.

```go
bytes("héllo").index(b'l')          // => 3 — h=0, é=1..2, l=3
bytes("héllo").index("llo")         // => 3
bytes("héllo").index_last(b'l')     // => 4
bytes("abc").index(b'z')            // => undefined
bytes("abc").index(b'z', -1)        // => -1 — only if you ask for it
```

<a id="index_last"></a>
### `index_last([x[, default]]) -> int`

Answer the last position of a match, or `undefined` (the `default` when given) on a miss; see [`index`](#index).

<a id="insert"></a>
### `insert(i, ...items) -> bytes`

Insert each argument as one element at position `i`.

`insert(i, ...items)` is `push` at a position; as a positional **edit**, `i` outside `[0, len]` raises (negative
`i` counts from the end).

```go
bytes("ad").insert(1, b'b', b'c')   // => bytes([97, 98, 99, 100])
bytes("ab").insert(3, b'x')         // Error: index_out_of_bounds: (insert) 3 out of range [0, 2]
```

<a id="insert_in_place"></a>
### `insert_in_place(i, ...items) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `insert`.

<a id="is_ascii"></a>
### `is_ascii() -> bool`

Report whether every octet is below `0x80`.

There is deliberately **no `is_valid()`**: every octet is a valid octet. The decode question is
`b.string().is_valid()`, asked of the type that can answer it.

<a id="is_empty"></a>
### `is_empty() -> bool`

Report whether the `bytes` value has no elements.

<a id="is_true"></a>
### `is_true() -> bool`

Report truthiness, which is non-emptiness: `!!x` ⟺ `x != bytes()`.

<a id="keep"></a>
### `keep(...x) -> bytes`

Keep only the matches of an element, a run, a set or a predicate; with no argument, the significant elements; see [`remove`](#remove).

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

<a id="keep_in_place"></a>
### `keep_in_place(...x) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `keep`.

<a id="last"></a>
### `last([default]) -> byte`

Answer the last element; an empty `bytes` raises unless a default is given.

<a id="len"></a>
### `len() -> int`

Answer the number of elements — octets, not symbols.

```go
bytes("héllo").len()        // => 6 — octets
```

<a id="map"></a>
### `map(fn) -> bytes`

Answer `bytes` of the callback's results, strictly 1:1: each result must be exactly one octet.

The callback gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`map` is strictly 1:1 and answers `bytes`: the callback must produce exactly **one element** — a byte, an ASCII
rune, or an int in `0`–`255`. A result outside the octet range raises (no silent wrap), and so does a sequence or
`undefined` result.

```go
bytes([1, 2, 3]).map(func(x) { return x.int() * 2 })    // => bytes([2, 4, 6])
bytes([200, 100]).map(func(x) { return x.int() * 2 })   // Error: invalid_value: an int ... must be in [0, 255], got 400
bytes("ab").map(func(x) { return 'é' })                 // Error: invalid_value — 2 octets do not fit one element
bytes("ab").map(func(x) { return "xy" })                // Error: invalid_value — map is 1:1; use flat_map
```

<a id="max"></a>
### `max([default]) -> byte`

Answer the largest element; an empty `bytes` raises unless a default is given.

<a id="min"></a>
### `min([default]) -> byte`

Answer the smallest element; an empty `bytes` raises unless a default is given.

<a id="pad_end"></a>
### `pad_end(n[, fill]) -> bytes`

Pad at the back with the fill element until length `n`; see [`pad_start`](#pad_start).

<a id="pad_end_in_place"></a>
### `pad_end_in_place(n[, fill]) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `pad_end`.

<a id="pad_start"></a>
### `pad_start(n[, fill]) -> bytes`

Pad at the front with the fill element until length `n`.

Width counts **octets**; the fill is exactly **one literal octet** (a run fill raises; so does a rune whose
encoding is more than one octet). Default fill is the space octet. A width at or below the length is a no-op;
one past `4294967296` octets raises rather than exhausting the host.

```go
bytes("42").pad_start(4, b'0')      // => bytes([48, 48, 52, 50])
bytes("é").pad_end(4, b'.')         // => bytes([195, 169, 46, 46]) — é already counts as 2
bytes("x").pad_start(3, 'é')        // Error: invalid_value — the fill does not fit a single element
bytes("x").pad_start(3, "ab")       // Error: invalid_argument_type — fill is one element
```

<a id="pad_start_in_place"></a>
### `pad_start_in_place(n[, fill]) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `pad_start`.

<a id="partition"></a>
### `partition(...seps) -> array`

Split at the first separator hit into exactly three pieces, `[before, sep, after]`.

A miss answers `[b, bytes(), bytes()]`. With no argument the separator is the whole first maximal run of blank
octets. Separators take the same menu as [`split`](#split); the pieces are `bytes`.

```go
bytes("k=v=w").partition("=")       // => [bytes([107]), bytes([61]), bytes([118, 61, 119])]
```

<a id="prepend"></a>
### `prepend(...xs) -> bytes`

Add the arguments at the front as whole operands, in argument order; see [`append`](#append).

<a id="prepend_in_place"></a>
### `prepend_in_place(...xs) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `prepend`.

<a id="push"></a>
### `push(...items) -> bytes`

Add each argument at the back as exactly **one element**; a sequence argument raises, even at length 1, and so does a multi-octet rune.

`push`/`push_first` are the validating forms: **one element per argument** — a sequence argument raises even at
length 1, and a multi-octet rune raises too (it does not fit one element).

```go
bytes("ab").push(98)                // => bytes([97, 98, 98]) — an in-range int is one octet
bytes("ab").push(b'\xff')           // => bytes([97, 98, 255])
bytes("ab").push('c')               // => bytes([97, 98, 99]) — ASCII rune = one octet
bytes("ab").push(256)               // Error: invalid_value: (push) an int reads as one octet and must be in [0, 255]
bytes("ab").push('é')               // Error: invalid_value: the value does not fit a single element (2 octets — use append)
bytes("ab").push("c")               // Error: invalid_argument_type — a sequence never reads as one element here
```

<a id="push_first"></a>
### `push_first(...items) -> bytes`

Add each argument at the front as exactly one element, in argument order; see [`push`](#push).

<a id="push_first_in_place"></a>
### `push_first_in_place(...items) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `push_first`.

<a id="push_in_place"></a>
### `push_in_place(...items) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `push`.

<a id="reduce"></a>
### `reduce(init, fn) -> value`

Fold the elements left to right into an accumulator that starts at `init`.

The callback gets `(acc, element)`, or `(acc, index, element)` when it does not accept two arguments
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

```go
bytes("abc").reduce(0, func(acc, x) { return acc + x.int() })           // => 294 — the checksum spelling
```

<a id="remove"></a>
### `remove(...x) -> bytes`

Remove every match of an element, a run, a set or a predicate; with no argument, the elements of the [blank set](#the-blank-set).

A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](#callbacks)).

`remove` and [`keep`](#keep) both take the full menu and act on every occurrence; a miss is a silent no-op.

```go
bytes("banana").keep(b'a')        // => bytes([97, 97, 97])
bytes("banana").remove("an")        // => bytes([98, 97])
```

<a id="remove_in_place"></a>
### `remove_in_place(...x) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `remove`.

<a id="remove_prefix"></a>
### `remove_prefix(x, ...more) -> bytes`

Remove the element or run — or the longest of a set of them — once, anchored at the front; absent → unchanged.

The element or run is removed once — of a set, the longest that matches — and a miss answers the receiver
unchanged.

```go
bytes("foobar").remove_prefix("foo")        // => bytes([98, 97, 114])
```

<a id="remove_prefix_in_place"></a>
### `remove_prefix_in_place(x, ...more) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `remove_prefix`.

<a id="remove_suffix"></a>
### `remove_suffix(x, ...more) -> bytes`

Remove the element or run — or the longest of a set of them — once, anchored at the back; absent → unchanged; see [`remove_prefix`](#remove_prefix).

<a id="remove_suffix_in_place"></a>
### `remove_suffix_in_place(x, ...more) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `remove_suffix`.

<a id="repeat"></a>
### `repeat(n) -> bytes`

Concatenate the receiver with itself `n` times; `b * n` is the operator form.

`repeat(n)` takes a whole-number count (`1.5` raises) and has the operator form `b * n` (no reflected `n * b`).

```go
bytes("ab").repeat(2)           // => bytes([97, 98, 97, 98])
bytes("ab").repeat(1.5)         // Error: invalid_value — never silent truncation
```

<a id="replace"></a>
### `replace(old, new) -> bytes`

Replace every occurrence of `old`, an element or a run, with `new`.

Element or run in both positions; every occurrence, leftmost, non-overlapping.

```go
bytes("a-b-c").replace(b'-', " / ")     // => bytes([97, 32, 47, 32, 98, 32, 47, 32, 99])
```

<a id="replace_in_place"></a>
### `replace_in_place(old, new) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `replace`.

<a id="reverse"></a>
### `reverse() -> bytes`

Reverse the order of the elements.

<a id="reverse_in_place"></a>
### `reverse_in_place() -> bytes`

In-place twin of `reverse`.

<a id="runes"></a>
### `runes([default]) -> runes`

Decode the octets as `runes`; an octet that is not a symbol becomes its escape.

```go
bytes("hé").runes()         // => u"hé"
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="slice"></a>
### `slice([start[, end]]) -> bytes`

Answer a copy of the elements from `start` to `end`; bounds **clamp** (contrast `splice`, which raises), negative indices count from the end.

`slice(i, j)` **clamps**.

```go
bytes("abc").slice(1, 99)       // => bytes([98, 99]) — clamps
```

<a id="slice_view"></a>
### `slice_view([start[, end]]) -> bytes`

Answer the elements from `start` to `end` as a view sharing the receiver's storage, so mutation flows both ways.

The sharing twin of [`slice`](#slice).

```go
sv := bytes("abcdef")
v := sv.slice_view(1, 3)        // shares storage
v[0] = b'X'                     // sv is now bytes([97, 88, 99, 100, 101, 102])
```

<a id="sort"></a>
### `sort() -> bytes`

Sort the octets by value; there is no comparator.

```go
bytes("cba").sort()             // => bytes([97, 98, 99])
```

<a id="sort_in_place"></a>
### `sort_in_place() -> bytes`

In-place twin of `sort`.

<a id="splice"></a>
### `splice([start[, delete_count]]) -> bytes` / `splice(start, delete_count, ...items) -> bytes`

Removes `delete_count` elements at `start`, then inserts the items there.

`splice(start[, count, ...items])` is the positional edit: `start` outside `[0, len]` raises, a negative `count`
raises, the `count` clamps; the inserts take the add-side reading (runs spread, elements insert).

```go
bytes("abcd").splice(1, 2, "XY")    // => bytes([97, 88, 89, 100])
bytes("ab").splice(3, 0)        // Error: index_out_of_bounds: (splice, start index) 3 out of range [0, 2]
```

<a id="splice_in_place"></a>
### `splice_in_place([start[, delete_count]]) -> bytes` / `splice_in_place(start, delete_count, ...items) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `splice`.

<a id="split"></a>
### `split(...seps) -> array`

Split the octets into an array of the pieces between the separators.

Separators from the dispatch menu: element, run, homogeneous variadic set, element-level predicate, or absent
(= the blank set). **Explicit separators keep empty pieces** (n hits → n+1 pieces); the no-arg blank form drops
empties; an empty-run separator matches nothing. No limit argument exists. The pieces are `bytes`.

```go
bytes("a,,b").split(b',')           // => [bytes([97]), bytes([]), bytes([98])] — empties kept
bytes("a::b").split("::")           // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98])]
bytes("a,b;c").split(b',', b';')    // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]
bytes("a,b").split(b',', "::")      // Error: invalid_argument_type — mixed element + run set
bytes("a1b2c").split(func(x) { return x >= b'0' && x <= b'9' })
                                    // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]
bytes("ab").split("")               // => [bytes([97, 98])] — an empty run matches nothing
```

<a id="split_lines"></a>
### `split_lines() -> array`

Split the octets into an array of lines at `\n`, `\r\n` or `\r`; a trailing line break adds no empty last line.

```go
bytes("a\nb\r\nc").split_lines()    // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]
```

<a id="string"></a>
### `string([default]) -> string`

Decode the octets as a `string`; an octet that is not a symbol becomes its escape.

```go
bytes("héllo").string()     // => "héllo"
bytes([255]).string()       // => "\xff" — the octet's escape — never raises, never loses it
```

The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

<a id="trim"></a>
### `trim(...set) -> bytes`

Repeatedly drop the elements at both ends while they belong to the set (the blank set with no argument).

A **set of elements**, stripped while they repeat at the edge; a run argument raises (the anchored run form is
`remove_prefix`/`remove_suffix`); no arguments = the blank set.

```go
bytes("xxhixx").trim(b'x')          // => bytes([104, 105])
bytes("xyhi").trim("xy")            // Error: invalid_argument_type: trim takes a set of elements, not a run
```

<a id="trim_end"></a>
### `trim_end(...set) -> bytes`

Drop the trailing elements that belong to the set (the blank set with no argument); see [`trim`](#trim).

<a id="trim_end_in_place"></a>
### `trim_end_in_place(...set) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `trim_end`.

<a id="trim_in_place"></a>
### `trim_in_place(...set) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `trim`.

<a id="trim_start"></a>
### `trim_start(...set) -> bytes`

Drop the leading elements that belong to the set (the blank set with no argument); see [`trim`](#trim).

<a id="trim_start_in_place"></a>
### `trim_start_in_place(...set) -> bytes`

In-place twin of `trim_start`.

<a id="unique"></a>
### `unique() -> bytes`

Drop repeats, keeping each element at its first occurrence.

```go
bytes("aabbaa").unique()        // => bytes([97, 98])
```

<a id="unique_in_place"></a>
### `unique_in_place() -> bytes`

In-place twin of `unique`.
